title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: reading the day, ordering the past, writing the letter

questions.prompt: A hostel pins this notice up in its hall. "SATURDAY — two guided walks, and you choose one. The LAKE WALK leaves at 8.00, follows the shore for nine kilometres and is back for lunch. The RIDGE WALK leaves at 7.00, climbs through the pine wood and comes home around the far side of the hill; it is four kilometres longer, and walkers on it are asked never to step off the marked path. Both walks are free for guests of the hostel. There is no water on either route, so fill your bottle before you leave." Which statements does the notice let you check?

options.text: The ridge walk covers more ground than the lake walk.
The ridge walk sets off earlier than the lake walk.
Walkers on the lake walk are told to keep to a marked path.
Guests of the hostel pay nothing for either walk.
The ridge walk is back at the hostel in time for lunch.

questions.explanation: A notice like this one is scanned, not read like a story, and every claim about the two walks is held against its own lines. It gives the ridge walk as four kilometres longer, so that walk does cover more ground. It prints 7.00 against 8.00, so the ridge walk does set off first. And it says both walks are free for guests of the hostel, so a guest pays nothing either way. The two others fail, and they fail differently. The instruction never to step off the marked path is attached to the ridge walk alone, so putting it on the lake walk moves an instruction from one walk to the other. And the notice gives a return time for the lake walk only: it never says when the ridge walk comes home, so claiming it is back in time for lunch is not reading the notice but filling in a gap the notice left. What a notice does not say is not yours to assume.

questions.prompt: Complete: "The lighthouse is the ___ point the coast walk reaches."

options.text: farest
farther
furthest
most far

questions.explanation: The sentence puts the lighthouse at the end point of the whole walk, so it needs a superlative, and far builds its superlative irregularly as the furthest, or the farthest: the "furthest" point the coast walk reaches. "farther" is the comparative of far and would set the lighthouse against one other place, which the sentence never names. "most far" applies the rule of long adjectives to a word of one syllable that has its own irregular forms. "farest" invents a regular -est on a word that refuses it, in the same way as goodest would.

questions.prompt: Read: "The guide had explained the route twice before anybody asked a question." Which sentence keeps exactly the same order of events?

options.text: The guide explained the route twice after somebody had asked a question.
Before the guide explained the route twice, somebody asked a question.
After somebody asked a question, the guide explained the route twice.
After the guide explained the route twice, somebody asked a question.

questions.explanation: In the original, the explaining carries the past perfect and before puts the question after it, so the guide spoke first and the question came second. Turning before into after means turning the two halves round as well, which gives "After the guide explained the route twice, somebody asked a question." — and once after is there the order is written on the page, so the past perfect is no longer needed. "After somebody asked a question, the guide explained the route twice." keeps after but leaves the halves where they were, and so reverses the order. "Before the guide explained the route twice, somebody asked a question." keeps before and reverses it too. "The guide explained the route twice after somebody had asked a question." moves the past perfect onto the question, which makes the question the earlier of the two.

questions.prompt: Complete: "For a driver in a hurry the mountain route is ___ than the coast road, but it is far more beautiful."

options.text: a bit badder
a bit worse
much worst
very worse

questions.explanation: The sentence compares two roads and goes on with than, so it needs a comparative; the comparative of bad is the irregular worse, and a comparative may be weakened by a bit: "a bit worse" than the coast road. "a bit badder" builds a regular -er on bad, which has its own form and refuses one. "much worst" picks the superlative, and a superlative cannot stand in a sentence that continues with than. "very worse" gets the comparative right and then puts very in front of it, the one modifier English never allows there; much, far, a lot and a bit are the words that do the job.

questions.prompt: A traveller has finished listing everything that went wrong during her week and is writing the last part of her letter to a company she has never dealt with. Which sentence belongs there?

options.text: Give me my money back straight away.
I would be grateful if you would refund part of what I paid.
You must pay me back, or I shall never travel with you again.
I am wondering whether you might possibly consider some kind of refund.

questions.explanation: The third part of the plan states what the writer expects from the company, and to a stranger it has to be firm and polite in the same breath, which is what "I would be grateful if you would refund part of what I paid." does: it names the thing asked for and asks for it courteously. "Give me my money back straight away." is an order, and an order to a company you have never dealt with reads as rudeness rather than firmness. "You must pay me back, or I shall never travel with you again." adds a threat, which puts the reader on the defensive instead of moving him to act. "I am wondering whether you might possibly consider some kind of refund." is polite but hides behind so many hedges that it never says clearly what is wanted, and a third part that states no expectation does not do its job.

questions.prompt: Read this short account. "The coach broke down forty kilometres from the resort we had booked, and the driver told us we would sleep in the nearest village. My sister cried for an hour. The family who kept the village café had already heard about us by the time we walked in, and they opened two rooms above the kitchen. We stayed four days instead of one, and when the coach was mended none of us wanted to get on it." Which title fits the account best?

options.text: The four days we never booked
How to choose a resort
A breakdown that spoilt the holiday
The night my sister cried

questions.explanation: A title has to hold the whole account, and this one runs from a breakdown on the road to four days nobody wanted to leave: "The four days we never booked" names both ends of that movement, the stop that was never planned and the stay it turned into. "A breakdown that spoilt the holiday" fits the first line and contradicts the last, since the travellers stayed on and then refused to board the mended coach. "The night my sister cried" is true, and it is the most striking detail in the account, but it covers one hour out of four days: that is a caption under a photograph, not a title over a text. "How to choose a resort" announces a guide that gives advice, and the account gives none — it tells what happened to one family that in the end chose nothing at all.
